purpose: Structured FTC Doxo bill-payment route ledger linking search/channel confusion, alleged fees and payment timing risk, and a pending proposed institutional response while preserving bill status, service continuity, redress, and switching as open.

events.geography: United States; Doxo online bill-payment users and utility, car-loan, and other bill routes
events.date_precision: Complaint filed April 25, 2024; proposed stipulated order and case-page update dated August 17, 2026; underlying user episodes are not individually dated
events.denominator: One named FTC enforcement case; cited internal heavy-user survey and complaint contacts are selected case evidence, not a representative household denominator
events.method: Structured extraction from the official FTC complaint, internal-survey reference, settlement announcement, filed stipulated proposed order, and case-page status
events.missingness: No user identifier, search exposure, biller, fee amount, consent record, payment success, bill status, service continuity, individual relief, or later switching is retained
events.exposure: The FTC complaint alleges that search ads and landing pages could make Doxo appear affiliated with or necessary for bill payment, while adding delivery fees and recurring subscription terms
events.alternatives_before_action: Consumers could pay the direct biller, use another intermediary, mail a check, use a bank or card route, or not complete payment; the feasible alternative and selected route are not observed per person
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: The alleged route can move cost into fees, subscription charges, affiliation uncertainty, cancellation effort, and payment-timing risk; convenience for some users remains a counterinterpretation
events.choice_or_response: The cited internal survey reports that approximately 30% of heavy users falsely thought Doxo was the only way to pay bills; complaint contacts and user route choices are not a representative use or non-use measure
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Doxo controlled search presentation, affiliation claims, fees, payment routing, subscription disclosures, and cancellation; billers and consumers retained different alternative-route powers
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: The FTC case page lists a filed stipulated proposed order with proposed $2.1 million monetary-judgment terms, permanent disclosure/consent/cancellation controls, and possible consumer-relief use; the case remains pending and distribution is unobserved
events.immediate_outcome: Search-route confusion, alleged fee mechanisms, and a proposed institutional-control response are visible at case level
events.protected_outcome: Clearer affiliation, total-cost, consent, and cancellation disclosures could improve future informed payment choice; no individual bill or service outcome is established
events.sacrificed_outcome: Avoidable fees, time, late charges, arrears, insurance lapse, or utility interruption are alleged in the complaint but cannot be assigned to a person or verified from this record
events.cost_risk_transfer: An intermediary can shift payment, timing, and recourse risk from billers or platforms to households; the proposed controls may shift some compliance responsibility back to the firm
events.later_outcome: Payment success, biller posting, late fees, service continuity, correction/refund, redress receipt, trust, direct-biller use, and switching remain open
events.meaning_and_attribution: The FTC attributes alleged deception and fee practices to Doxo, but consumer-level fairness, blame, legitimacy, and trust change are not measured
events.public_or_collective_response: FTC enforcement is observed; consumer organizing, complaint persistence, political action, and collective response are not linked
events.counterexample: A consumer may knowingly choose Doxo for convenience and complete payment successfully; alleged confusion and downstream risk do not establish universal harm
events.source_and_uncertainty: Official complaint and proposed settlement materials; internal survey and complaint contacts are selected, allegations are not person-level incidence or service-failure estimates, and proposed relief is not completed distribution

arrows.evidence: The FTC alleges search ads and landing pages could make Doxo appear connected to billers; its cited internal survey reports approximately 30% of heavy users falsely thought Doxo was the only payment route
arrows.counterexample: The survey is internal and selected, and the complaint does not establish what each consumer saw or believed
arrows.remaining_gap: User-level exposure, search result, affiliation belief, biller, language, and direct-biller awareness

arrows.to: fee, subscription, cancellation, and payment-timing burden
arrows.evidence: The complaint alleges add-on delivery fees, recurring subscription terms, and immediate consumer charges while paper checks could reach billers days or weeks later
arrows.counterexample: A fee may have been knowingly accepted and the payment may still have posted on time; the complaint does not identify individual consent or outcome
arrows.remaining_gap: Fee amount, consent, cancellation effort, payment timestamp, biller posting, and alternative route

arrows.to: late fee, arrears, insurance lapse, utility interruption, or other household consequence
arrows.evidence: The complaint alleges that some consumers experienced utility shutoffs, insurance lapses, fees, or fines despite believing they paid on time
arrows.counterexample: The complaint supplies no person-level denominator or verified biller, shutoff, lapse, fee, or fine record
arrows.remaining_gap: Identifier-linked payment success, bill status, service continuity, late charges, and household outcome

arrows.to: proposed FTC disclosure, consent, and cancellation controls
arrows.evidence: The filed stipulated proposed order sets permanent controls for affiliation, fees, total cost, negative-option terms, cancellation, and financial-information use
arrows.counterexample: The case page remains pending; proposed terms do not establish court entry, implementation, or compliance
arrows.remaining_gap: Final order status, installment completion, compliance monitoring, and realized disclosure behavior

arrows.to: consumer redress, restored bill security, trust, or switching
arrows.evidence: The public record permits possible consumer-relief use but does not identify eligibility, distribution, bill correction, service continuity, trust, or provider switching
arrows.counterexample: A control can improve future choice without restoring prior fees or time, while a consumer may stay because direct alternatives are costly
arrows.remaining_gap: Distribution, receipt, refund/correction, residual loss, direct-biller use, trust, and switching reason

boundary: This ledger formalizes a named bill-payment route from search/channel confusion through alleged fee and timing risk to a pending proposed institutional response. It does not estimate household fee incidence, payment failure, service interruption, remedy receipt, or switching.
storage_boundary: No consumer account, bill, payment, or service file is retained; only bounded official case evidence, selected-survey limits, proposed controls, and open links are represented.
